To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) MHCII expression in the absence of the promoter complex can be induced in professional APCs and is sufficient to support T cell activation; (b) the inducible pathway is genetically independent of known promoter elements; and (c) the inducibility of MHCII expression may provide an alternative treatment option for patients with MHCII deficiency.
MHCII expression through a hither to unknown pathway supports Th-cell-dependent immune responses.
1) residual MHCII on professional APCs is sufficient to support T helper cell activation and 2) an alternative MHC class II expression pathway exists in mice.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the elucidation of the molecular mechanisms that regulate MHCII expression and the development of T helper cells and provides a basis for the development of new treatment strategies for patients with BLS.
an alternative pathway of MHCII expression, which is independent of the classical promoter complex and supports Th-cell-dependent immunity.
the discovery of a new MHCII expression mechanism and its implications for MHCII-deficient patients.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the RFX complex is a transcriptional repressor of MHCII in the absence of its activator CIITA, and that this repressor function is relieved in the presence of Th lymphocytes.

MHC class II expression is not only controlled by the known transcriptional machinery, but that an alternative pathway is also present, and that the RFX transcription factors are not only activators, but also repressors.
MHCII expression in BLS can be supported by a hitherto unappreciated pathway, which is independent of the RFX and CIITA proteins and which may be of therapeutic relevance for patients with BLS.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the MHCII pathway can be divided into three parts, a constitutive and a repressive part, and an inducible part.
MHCII expression in the context of BLS is regulated by two independent pathways.
MHCII deficiency is a disease of MHCII expression rather than MHCII function.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the residual MHCII expressed on the surface of professional APCs is sufficient to support Th-cell activation.
MHCII expression can occur in the absence of the known promoter and that this pathway can support Th-cell-dependent immune responses.
MHCII expression through the alternative pathway can be sufficient to restore Th-cell-dependent immunity.
